newsitem.title: USA: House panel probes data purging by NASD - aide.
newsitem.headline: House panel probes data purging by NASD - aide.

text.p: A key U.S. House panel chairman has directed his staff to probe charges that the National Association of Securities Dealers "caused the purging" of thousands of pieces of disciplinary data on the nation's securities brokers, a spokesman said on Friday.

"Chairman Bliley is very troubled by the news," the aide to Rep. Thomas Bliley, R-Va., chairman of the House Commerce Committee, said in a telephone interview. "He has directed the staff to conduct an inquiry at once."

The Wall Street Journal reported on February 7 that as many as 20,000 pieces of data were deleted from NASD's central registration depository (CRD), the computer system that investors and federal and state regulators use to track the disciplinary histories of stock and bond dealers and their firms.

"Clearly this is a subject for concern," added Bliley's spokesman, Michael Collins, communications director for the panel. "These are records that investors count on. Obviously, these records need to have integrity."
NASD officials say that only about 3,000 pieces of information were deleted and deletions were unintentional. But state regulators insist it is 20,000, the Journal said.

Elisse Walter, chief operating officer of NASDR, the association's new regulatory arm, said data was "mistakenly removed" from one of the NASD's data bases She said NASD has been negotiating with with state regulators for months on the issue.
Walter told Reuters that NASD, by policy, does not release the data at issue to investors.
The data includes customer complaints, arbitration actions, and civil lawsuits that are never resolved because investors withdraw them early or they are dismissed by courts or arbitration panels.
But the CRD system is partly run by state securities departments. And some states make such information available to investors on request, she said.

Walter stressed that the information is not lost. It was inadvertently removed from the CRD system and placed elsewhere at NASD's technical office in Rockville, Md., said Walter, who was not on board at NASD when the files were removed.

An NASD's spokesman said, "We have finally come to agreement with the North American Securities Administrators Association on what information needs to be put back in the system. The process is beginning immediately."
Lawyers for Theresa Carr, a former senior compliance examiner at NASD who is suing the association, called NASD's data problem a "fiasco."
"It's proof that the nation's self-regulatory sytem, which dates back to the late 1930s, in in dire need of an overhaul," said New York-based Singer Zamansky in a press statement.

Carr filed a $20 million damages suit against NASD last September charging she was pushed out as senior compliance examiner at the group's New York City office because of her aggressive investigation of the municipal bond market.
